title: Refundable Investment Tax Credit - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Learn how a Refundable Investment Tax Credit provides cash flow to qualifying Canadian businesses in our SR&ED tax glossary.
summary: A refundable investment tax credit (ITC) under Canada's federal SR&ED program lets eligible claimants receive unused credits in cash. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations receive a 100% refund of the 35% enhanced ITC on current expenditures within the $6 million limit, but only 40% on capital expenditures.

body.text: A refundable investment tax credit (ITC) under Canada's federal SR&ED program lets eligible claimants receive unused credits in cash. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations receive a 100% refund of the 35% enhanced ITC on current expenditures within the $6 million limit, but only 40% on capital expenditures.

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive regime—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under the Income Tax Act (ITA) and complemented by provincial tax credits and direct innovation contributions—has undergone its most substantial legislative and administrative overhaul in over a decade between December 2024 and November 2026. Under Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Parliament enacted major retroactive enhancements for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024: doubling the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable investment tax credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (superseding the interim $4.5 million proposal from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement), raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% enhanced credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out (which Canadian-controlled private corporations [CCPCs] may also elect to use), and restoring pre-2014 eligibility for SR&ED capital expenditures and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process alongside artificial-intelligence-driven risk triage to deliver upfront technical eligibility determinations for businesses earning under $25 million in gross business income.

On November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 tabled a Notice of Ways and Means Motion proposing—for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—to expand SR&ED beyond experimental development to cover initial regulatory approval and certification testing as well as intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance expenses (subject to disposition recapture), while leaving a previously consulted federal patent box unimplemented. Provincial innovation tax regimes have shifted concurrently: Québec abolished eight legacy R&D tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 in favour of the consolidated 20% to 30% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) while retaining its 2.0% effective-rate Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI) IP box; British Columbia enacted Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) to align its 10% refundable credit with the federal $6 million limit and ECPC expansion while making the credit permanent; industry tax directories report that Saskatchewan doubled its CCPC refundable ceiling from $1 million to $2 million effective December 16, 2024; and Ontario automatically restored capital equipment eligibility from December 16, 2024 upon Bill C-15's Royal Assent while keeping its separate $3 million cap and dual phase-out grinds on the 8% Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC).
1. Legislative Architecture and Statutory Foundations of Canadian R&D Tax Law
Dual-Mechanism Structure Under the Income Tax Act

Under the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), as amended (the ITA), Canada delivers R&D tax relief to corporations, individuals (sole proprietorships), trusts, and partnerships conducting qualifying work in Canada through two distinct but linked statutory mechanisms. First, under section 37 of the ITA (specifically subsection 37(1), including paragraph 37(1)(b) for qualifying post-December 15, 2024 capital property), a taxpayer calculates allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year and adds them to a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Any available balance in the section 37 pool may be deducted to reduce net business income in the current taxation year or carried forward indefinitely to reduce net income in future taxation years. Second, under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) and related refundable credit provisions of the ITA, a claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) at either the 15% basic rate or the 35% enhanced rate on "qualified SR&ED expenditures". Unused SR&ED ITCs may be refunded in cash (where eligible for refundability), applied to reduce federal Part I income tax payable, carried back 3 taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years.
Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1) ITA

Every federal SR&ED claim—and every provincial R&D tax credit piggybacking on federal project qualification—stands or falls on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" falling within one of three core categories in paragraphs (a) through (c):

items: Basic Research (Paragraph (a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Applied Research (Paragraph (b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Experimental Development (Paragraph (c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

body.text: In assessing project scope, the CRA evaluates SR&ED at the level necessary to recognize all interrelated activities collectively required to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties and attempt a specific scientific or technological advancement, explicitly encompassing commensurate support work. Conversely, ordinary product development and post-experimental commercial activities are excluded from SR&ED eligibility under existing law (prior to the proposed Budget 2026 commercialization expansion). Ineligible activities include market research or sales promotion efforts, routine data collection, routine quality control or testing, cosmetic or stylistic modifications to existing products, non-technical project management or standard user-interface design, routine cloud migration, and research lacking a clear scientific or technological objective.
Chronological Audit of Federal Legislative and Administrative Reforms (2024–2026)

Corporate tax compliance and financial statement provisioning require distinguishing sharply among superseded 2024 proposals, binding statutory amendments enacted in March 2026, operational CRA administrative programs launched in April 2026, and un-enacted legislative proposals tabled in November 2026. Throughout 2024, the Department of Finance Canada conducted public consultations on modernizing the SR&ED program alongside a potential Canadian patent box regime. On December 16, 2024, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) proposed raising the enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, lifting the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% credit to ECPCs, and reinstating capital expenditure eligibility. Because FES 2024 was superseded before enactment, the $4.5 million cap never became law—yet several un-updated third-party practitioner articles in 2026 still erroneously cite $4.5 million.

On November 4, 2025, Federal Budget 2025 incorporated the FES 2024 structural reforms while increasing the enhanced 35% ITC annual expenditure limit further from the proposed $4.5 million to $6 million, retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Parliament enacted these reforms in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Six days later, on April 1, 2026, the CRA operationalized Budget 2025's administrative reforms by launching an optional Pre-Claim Approval process, deploying an SR&ED Client Portal, expanding artificial intelligence in program administration to shield low-risk claims from unnecessary audit interventions, and opening targeted consultations to review Form T661, backed by Spring Economic Update 2026 funding aimed at accelerating claim processing.

Most recently, on November 5, 2026, Federal Budget 2026 tabled a Notice of Ways and Means Motion proposing to expand SR&ED eligibility to initial regulatory approval/certification validation and IP protection costs for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026. Published commentary on Budget 2026 reports Department of Finance cost projections for this commercialization expansion at $930 million over five years and $235 million ongoing annually. As of November 15, 2026, these Budget 2026 measures remain proposed legislation awaiting a budget implementation bill and Royal Assent. Meanwhile, despite the 2024 consultations and 2025 election platform commitments, the federal government omitted a federal patent box regime from both Budget 2025 and Budget 2026.

body.text: 2. Federal SR&ED Rates, Thresholds, Corporate Eligibility, and Refundability Mechanics
Enhanced 35% Rate Versus Basic 15% Rate

Under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) of the ITA and the CRA SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, federal SR&ED ITCs are earned at either an enhanced rate of 35% or a basic (general) rate of 15%. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the enhanced 35% rate applied exclusively to CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures annually. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit to $6,000,000—increasing the maximum annual enhanced refundable federal credit on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000—and extended eligibility for the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) as well as Canadian-resident subsidiaries that are all or substantially owned by an ECPC. (Subsection 127(9) ITA sets out the statutory definition of an ECPC, and subsection 127(10.6) ITA sets out the ECPC expenditure limit based on the three-year gross revenue test.)

By contrast, the basic 15% ITC rate applies to corporations other than qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs (including foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries and public corporations exceeding the phase-out ceiling), qualified SR&ED expenditures of a CCPC or ECPC exceeding its available annual expenditure limit, sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts.
Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Associated-Group Rules

Under subsections 127(10.2), 127(10.21) and 127(10.3) of the ITA, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit must be shared across all corporations within an associated group and formally allocated on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). Unlike Ontario's provincial OITC, the federal SR&ED expenditure limit has no prior-year taxable income phase-out. Instead, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 limit phases out linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (up from the pre-December 16, 2024 CCPC band of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000) under two statutory tests.

Under the default CCPC test, the $6,000,000 limit begins to decrease once the associated group's taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000 and is eliminated at $75,000,000. Under the gross revenue test—which is mandatory for ECPCs and elective for CCPCs under Bill C-15—the $6,000,000 limit phases out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based on the total average annual gross revenue reflected in financial statements over the three preceding fiscal years for every corporation that is a member of the group in the current taxation year, regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout all three preceding years. Permitting CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue phase-out protects capital-intensive private biotechnology, clean-technology, and deep-tech corporations whose balance-sheet paid-up capital or debt exceeds $15 million while pre-commercial revenue remains low. Incorporating short-taxation-year proration under subsection 127(10.5) ITA, the group's annual federal expenditure limit (EL, in dollars) is:

where A represents either prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada (for non-electing CCPCs) or three-year average annual group financial-statement gross revenue (for ECPCs and electing CCPCs), and D represents the number of days in the taxation year. Special anti-duplication rules under subsection 127(10.5) ITA also govern where a corporation has multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year while associated with another corporation.
Refundability Matrix: Current Versus Capital Expenditures and Entity Status

Following Bill C-15's restoration of capital expenditures, a critical audit distinction governs cash refundability: capital expenditures do not earn a 100% cash refund even within the $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit. Under the CRA SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, refundability depends both on the nature of the expenditure (current expenditures and the Prescribed Proxy Amount [PPA] versus capital expenditures) and on whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" (subject to the qualifying income limit in section 4.2 of the policy) and not an "excluded corporation".

Specifically, a CCPC that is a qualifying corporation (and not an excluded corporation) receives a cash refund equal to 100% of the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on qualified current expenditures and PPA, 40% of the unclaimed balance of its 35% enhanced ITC earned on qualified capital expenditures (representing an immediate cash refund of 40% × 35% = 14% of eligible capital cost, with the remaining 21% ITC available as a non-refundable tax offset), and 40% of the unclaimed balance of its 15% basic ITC earned on qualified expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit (a 40% × 15% = 6% cash refund plus 9% non-refundable credit). By contrast, a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation still receives 100% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC for current expenditures and PPA and 40% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC for capital expenditures, but earns 0% refundability (strictly non-refundable) on any 15% basic ITC above its expenditure limit.

Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) access the enhanced 35% refundable credit up to their $6,000,000 expenditure limit (subject to applicable refundability limits between current and capital expenditures) and earn a non-refundable 15% basic ITC above that limit. Other corporations (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large public corporations) earn a strictly non-refundable 15% basic ITC. For individuals (sole proprietorships) and trusts, published practitioner summaries diverge on cash refundability—some describing the 15% individual/trust ITC as non-refundable and others noting partial cash refundability for individuals filing Form T2038(IND)—while partnerships compute SR&ED expenditures at the partnership level under subsection 96(1) ITA to deduct against partnership income and allocate the 15% ITC to eligible partners via Form T5013.

body.text: 3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Cost Inclusion Rules

Computing an SR&ED claim on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) proceeds in two stages: identifying total allowable SR&ED expenditures (Part 3 of Form T661) and applying statutory adjustments and reductions (Part 4 of Form T661) to arrive at qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for ITCs.
Salaries and Wages, Payroll Mandates, and Specified Employee Restrictions

Only employment salaries or wages subject to T4 payroll reporting for employees directly engaged in SR&ED qualify as SR&ED labour expenditures. Dividends paid to founders or shareholder-developers represent corporate profit distributions rather than employment remuneration and are 100% ineligible for SR&ED claims; similarly, salaries or wages purported to be paid to partners of a partnership are not allowable for tax purposes. Under Form T661 rules, salary or wages incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days of the taxation year-end (reported on line 315 of Form T661) cannot be claimed in that year; they become claimable in the subsequent taxation year when actually paid (line 310), except that prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (line 310) are permanently excluded from the PPA salary base. Where employees perform permissible SR&ED work outside Canada deemed to be incurred in Canada under subsection 37(1.4) of the ITA, those wages are segregated on lines 265, 307, and 309 of Form T661 (under paragraph 37(1.5)(b) of the ITA, the amount deemed incurred in Canada is capped at 10% of total salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada).

Heightened statutory caps apply to "specified employees" (segregated on line 305 for Canadian work and line 309 for permissible work outside Canada, and scrutinized closely by the CRA where founder pay exceeds market rates). (The detailed share-ownership and non-arm's-length definition of a specified employee is governed by the ITA and section 7.0 of the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy). Under the CRA Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the amount of a specified employee's salary or wages included in the PPA salary base is restricted to the lesser of (1) 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary or wages (excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and line 310 prior-year unpaid wages) multiplied by the percentage of time spent on SR&ED, and (2) 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no further proration if the individual was not a specified employee for part of that employment period):
Specified employee salary base = lesser of (75% × eligible salary or wages × % of time on SR&ED) and (2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365))

where A is the calendar-year YMPE and B is the number of days employed in the taxation year. Because the maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE) for 2026 is $74,600, the maximum full-year (365-day) PPA salary base per specified employee in 2026 is $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600), generating a maximum PPA of $102,575 (55% × $186,500). Furthermore, where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations (including deemed associated related individuals or partnerships) in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the combined total included across all associated salary bases cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 in 2026) and must be allocated via Form T1174.
Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Versus Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA and the Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, claimants choose annually on Form T661 between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method to account for SR&ED overhead. Claimants electing the Proxy Method cannot include actual SR&ED overhead and other directly attributable expenditures in their SR&ED claim (those remain deductible as ordinary business expenses in the year); instead, they compute a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the salary base (Part 5, Section B, line 820 of Form T661). For every employee (both non-specified and specified), the PPA salary base excludes taxable benefits, prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (line 310), remuneration based on profits, bonuses, and employer-paid related benefits. Crucially, the PPA is used strictly to earn the SR&ED ITC—it is not included in the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and is not deducted in computing taxable income.

To ensure total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specified statutory deductions do not exceed total business deductions for the year, the Income Tax Regulations impose an Overall Cap on the PPA:
PPA ≤ A − B − C

where A is total amounts deducted in calculating net business income for tax purposes for the year across all businesses of the claimant (including cost of goods sold); B is the sum of deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (such as capital cost allowance [CCA], interest, and bad debts), 24 (ceasing to carry on business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents or brokers), 37 (SR&ED expenditure deductions), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts); and C is expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building. As an operational rule of thumb, the Overall Cap will generally not restrict the PPA provided the claimant deducts more than $55 of qualifying non-SR&ED business expenses for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.

Conversely, claimants choosing the Traditional Method do not compute a salary base, PPA, or Overall Cap; instead, they must specifically track, substantiate, and allocate actual overhead and other expenditures (line 360 of Form T661) that are directly related and incremental to performing SR&ED—such as SR&ED travel and training, property taxes, maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment, and other eligible costs that would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out. Under the Traditional Method, qualifying overhead is both added to the section 37 deductible pool and eligible for the SR&ED ITC.

body.text: Materials, Cloud Computing Environments, Subcontractors, and Exclusions

Materials consumed (line 320 of Form T661) or materials transformed in performing SR&ED are claimed separately under both the Proxy and Traditional methods, qualifying at 100% for the section 37 deduction and 100% for the SR&ED ITC (subject to ITC recapture if claimed property is later sold or converted to commercial use). Canadian CPA practice commentary confirms that software and AI claimants routinely claim cloud computing expenses (such as AWS, Google Cloud Platform, or Microsoft Azure environments) used specifically for R&D experimentation, staging, and testing as materials consumed, whereas cloud infrastructure running customer-facing production workloads is ineligible.

External SR&ED contracting and non-salary outlays are governed by strict statutory adjustments in Part 4 of Form T661. First, amounts paid under an SR&ED contract to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier (generally excluding non-Canadian subcontractors) are backed out at 100% on line 528. Second, for arm's-length Canadian contractors performing SR&ED on the claimant's behalf (line 340) and third-party payments for SR&ED documented on Form T1263 (line 370), 100% is deductible under section 37, but only 80% qualifies for the SR&ED ITC—with 20% excluded on line 529 to strip out assumed contractor profit margins. Practitioner audit guidance emphasizes isolating the qualifying technical SR&ED portion of a vendor invoice (excluding project management, UI design, and routine build tasks) before applying the 80% rule, and structuring written statements of work to substantiate direction, supervision, technological uncertainty, and separation of SR&ED from commercial deliverables under the CRA's "for" versus "on behalf of" evaluation criteria. Third, non-arm's-length contracts do not earn the 80% contractor inclusion; instead, related parties use Form T1146 to transfer qualified SR&ED expenditures and Form T1145 under subsections 127(19) and 127(20) ITA to allocate contract assistance. Fourth, current expenditures other than salary or wages not paid within 180 days of the taxation year-end are excluded on line 520, and line 530 excludes expenditures disallowed by regulation, such as interest and financing costs and dues or fees for membership in a scientific or technical society or organization.
Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

After an eleven-year exclusion spanning January 1, 2014 through December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 restored pre-2014 SR&ED eligibility for depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for both the paragraph 37(1)(b) income deduction and the 15% or 35% SR&ED ITC. Under the CRA SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, qualifying capital expenditures are restricted to depreciable property (for which CCA could otherwise be claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a) ITA) in which the claimant acquires ownership or a leasehold interest—excluding property held as an agent or nominee, structures built on another person's land without ownership or leasehold rights, and all acquisitions of buildings or leasehold interests in buildings. Practitioner analyses confirm that specialized equipment, test rigs, and dedicated local AI/computing hardware must be intended for at least 90% use in SR&ED (disqualifying mixed-use commercial equipment), highlight subsection 127(11.2) ITA as amended by Bill C-15 regarding transitional ITC timing rules, and emphasize that 35% enhanced ITCs on capital property are only 40% refundable and remain subject to recapture upon disposition or commercial conversion.
4. Proposed Budget 2026 Commercialization Expansion and Capital Investment Synergies
Regulatory Validation and Intellectual Property Protection Under Budget 2026

To bridge the commercialization funding gap once experimental development concludes, Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) proposes—for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026—to expand SR&ED into two downstream commercialization categories, both strictly gated on a direct nexus to an otherwise eligible SR&ED project.

Under the first proposed stream, Regulatory and Certification Requirements, eligible SR&ED activities expand to include tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialize a product or process, provided those activities directly relate to a project eligible under existing SR&ED rules. Claimable expenditure categories mirror existing SR&ED rules, encompassing wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead costs, and machinery and equipment.

Under the second proposed stream, Intellectual Property (IP) Protection, eligible SR&ED expenditures expand to cover reasonable expenses incurred to prepare and file registration applications, plus periodic maintenance fees payable to keep IP rights in force, for IP developed in the course of conducting an eligible SR&ED project. Protection is restricted to four specific forms of IP under Canadian legislation or equivalent foreign legislation: patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software. Geographically, official administrative fees paid to foreign IP offices outside Canada qualify, whereas supporting activities (such as preparing and drafting an application) qualify only if conducted in Canada. Costs to enforce IP rights—including infringement litigation—and costs not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP rights remain excluded. Crucially, if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED IP-protection support was claimed, recapture rules will reverse and claw back the related SR&ED income deductions and ITCs.
Interaction With Accelerated CCA, the Productivity Mega Deduction, and the Canada Growth Incentive

Corporations acquiring R&D or mixed-use equipment must coordinate SR&ED capital claims with broader capital expensing measures enacted in Bill C-15 and proposed in Budget 2026. Under Bill C-15, 100% immediate CCA expensing applies to qualifying purchases of patents (Class 44), data network infrastructure equipment (Class 46), and computer equipment and system software (Class 50) acquired on or after April 16, 2024 and available for use before January 1, 2027, alongside temporary immediate expensing for manufacturing and processing buildings. Extending Budget 2025's "Productivity Super-Deduction," Budget 2026 proposes a permanent Productivity Mega Deduction ($36 billion estimated fiscal cost over five years starting in 2026–27); commentary on Budget 2026 reports that this provides permanent immediate year-one write-offs for roughly two-thirds of capital assets acquired on or after September 15, 2026 (cutting Canada's marginal effective tax rate on new investment from 13.0% to 6.4%), though for pre-profit startups immediate CCA only builds non-capital loss carryforwards rather than delivering refundable cash like SR&ED.

Concurrently, Budget 2026 proposes the Canada Growth Incentive: a capital gains exemption of up to $15,000,000 per individual per business on newly issued qualifying shares of a CCPC issued for cash or qualifying employment services on or after November 5, 2026 and before 2037. To qualify, the carrying value of assets of the CCPC and related corporations cannot exceed $100,000,000 immediately before and after issuance, the qualifying business must be carried on primarily in Canada for at least 24 consecutive months after issuance, and the investor must hold the shares for at least 36 consecutive months before disposition (at which time the corporation must be resident in Canada and either a private corporation or a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada). For Alternative Minimum Tax purposes, 30% of the exempt gain would be included, and claims mutually reduce the Lifetime Capital Gains Exemption (which Bill C-15 raised to $1,250,000 effective June 25, 2024 with indexation resuming in 2026) on the same corporation except on qualifying sales to an Employee Ownership Trust or worker cooperative.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Commercialization Incentives

Outside Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA via Schedules filed with the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. Because provinces responded unevenly to Bill C-15's $6,000,000 expenditure limit and ECPC expansion, jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction verification is essential.
Québec: Replacement of Eight Legacy Credits by the CRIC and the IDCI IP Box

In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget tabled on March 25, 2025 (Information Bulletin 2025-6), the Ministère des Finances du Québec overhauled provincial R&D taxation for taxation years (or fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing eight separate legacy tax measures—including the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly 14% to 30%), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (with transitional relief through December 31, 2029 for existing fee balances), and the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services—and replacing them with the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC).

Administered by Revenu Québec, the CRIC is 100% refundable for any corporation (or corporate member of a qualified partnership) maintaining an establishment and carrying on business in Québec, regardless of corporate size or foreign/public ownership. Rather than scaling by corporate assets, CRIC rates scale by spending volume above an annual exclusion threshold: 30% refundable on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations), and 20% refundable on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 bracket. Crucially, CRIC covers both R&D and pre-commercialization activities constituting a continuation of Québec R&D—specifically prototype testing, validation processes, and studies for regulatory marketing approvals/certifications, plus product design (shape, aesthetics, functionality improvements, and material selection). Qualified expenditures comprise 100% of Québec employee salaries and wages, 100% of eligible capital equipment acquisition costs (subject to large-investment-project tax-holiday restrictions), and 50% of eligible subcontracting contracts (including universities, public research centres, and certified consortia). The annual exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum across eligible employees of Québec's personal income tax basic personal amount—$18,571 in 2025 and indexed by 2.05% to $18,952 in 2026—prorated by time spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization work. Because CRIC cannot be combined with other Québec credits (such as C3i or the modernized e-business/AI credit CDAEIA, which provides 30% total assistance split 22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026, stepping to 20%/10% by 2028, and halved starting in 2026 where ≥50% of gross revenue derives from related-party outsourcing used exclusively outside Québec) on the same expense, Québec tech firms must optimize expense allocation across programs.

For downstream commercialization income, Québec maintains Canada's sole statutory IP box: the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI), claimed on Form CO-737.18.CI. Qualifying Québec corporations commercializing a qualified IP asset (a patent, certificate of supplementary protection, copyrighted software, or plant breeders' rights variety resulting wholly or partly from Québec R&D) enjoy an effective Québec corporate tax rate of 2.0%—a 9.5 percentage point reduction from the 11.5% general rate—on qualified IP profits (from sales/leases of goods embedding the IP, intrinsically linked services, royalties, or judicial infringement damages, apportioned by a Québec R&D expenditure nexus ratio).
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC, and Non-Alignment With the Federal $6M Cap

Under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), Ontario corporations access three CRA-administered R&D tax credits. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566, Schedule 5 line 468) provides an 8% refundable credit exclusively to qualifying CCPCs with an Ontario permanent establishment performing SR&ED in Ontario. Ontario did not adopt Bill C-15's $6,000,000 limit or ECPC expansion for the OITC: the OITC remains capped at an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (maximum annual credit $240,000), shared among associated corporations, leaving Ontario CCPC SR&ED spending between $3 million and $6 million eligible for the 35% federal credit without an OITC top-up. Moreover, the $3,000,000 OITC limit undergoes two simultaneous multiplicative straight-line grinds based on the prior-year associated group: one between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income, and a second between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year specified/taxable capital. Practitioner modelling confirms these two survival ratios multiply when both apply (e.g., at $700,000 prior-year taxable income [1/3 survival = $1,000,000] and $30,000,000 taxable capital [80% survival], the remaining OITC limit is $1,000,000 × 80% = $800,000, or $64,000 maximum credit).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit to all corporations (including non-CCPCs and CCPCs claiming alongside or above the OITC), with no expenditure limit and a 3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward against Ontario corporate tax. Because Ontario designates the OITC as government assistance for ORDTC purposes, a CCPC claiming both must deduct its 8% OITC from the Ontario expenditure pool before multiplying by 3.5%. Third, under section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 and 569, Schedule 5 line 470) delivers a 20% refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 annually of qualified current SR&ED contract expenditures (maximum $4,000,000 annual credit per associated group) paid to an unconsolidated/non-connected Ontario Eligible Research Institute (universities, colleges, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, Networks of Centres of Excellence, or designated non-profits). Finally, Ontario practitioner reviews confirm that Bill C-15's Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 automatically restored 100% capital expenditure eligibility for both the OITC and ORDTC on depreciable SR&ED property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (subject to a 23.56% ORDTC recapture rule on commercial conversion or sale), even though ontario.ca web pages still displayed legacy post-2013 exclusion text as late as October 30, 2026.
British Columbia, Alberta, Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, under Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (following B.C. Budget 2026 on February 17, 2026), the province fully harmonized with Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024: qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs claim a 10% refundable credit up to the $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit (phased out between $15 million and $75 million), while other qualifying corporations and excess expenditures earn a 10% non-refundable credit (less refundable and renounced amounts) on Form T666 (Schedule 425). While B.C.'s program had previously been extended to September 1, 2027, 2026 tax directories report B.C. Budget 2026 removed its sunset to make the credit permanent.

In Alberta, Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) independently administers the refundable Innovation Employment Grant (IEG): practitioner and tax-software guides confirm an 8% base rate up to the corporation's prior two-year average Alberta R&D spending and a 20% incremental rate on spending above that two-year average, capped at $4,000,000 of annual eligible expenditures and eliminated once taxable capital reaches $50,000,000. Alberta IEG claims are filed on AT1 Schedule 29 (mapping to line 557 of Form T661 for tax years ending after December 15, 2024) within an absolute provincial deadline of 21 months after fiscal year-end.

In Manitoba, CRA's official program page confirms a 15% R&D tax credit (Schedule 380, Schedule 5 lines 606 and 613) with no federal-style expenditure cap, covering eligible Manitoba current and depreciable capital expenditures (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings): R&D under an eligible institute contract is 100% refundable, whereas in-house R&D is 50% refundable (7.5%) and 50% non-refundable (7.5%), with a 20-year carryforward and an elective renunciation option under subsection 7.3(7) of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba). In Saskatchewan, corporations claim a 10% credit on Schedule 403; industry tax credit directories report Saskatchewan doubled its CCPC refundable ceiling from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 effective December 16, 2024 (10% non-refundable above that limit and for non-CCPCs), subject to a $1,000,000 annual credit cap. Across Atlantic and Northern Canada, Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301 / Form T1129) each provide a 15% refundable R&D tax credit, while Yukon (Schedule 442) provides a 15% refundable credit plus an extra 5% (20% total) on amounts paid to Yukon University. Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut have no separate statutory R&D tax credit listed in national compendia, relying solely on federal SR&ED and direct grants.

body.text: 6. Direct R&D Grants, Government Assistance Grinding, and Multi-Program Stacking Mathematics
Direct Federal R&D Funding Pillars: NRC IRAP and the Strategic Innovation Fund

Whereas SR&ED is a retrospective, non-competitive entitlement claimed after fiscal year-end, federal direct R&D grants require prospective approval before incurring project costs. For incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer full-time-equivalent (FTE) employees globally, the primary direct R&D vehicle is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), whose published decision service standards cover non-repayable contributions up to $10,000,000. While audits of official NRC pages emphasize that NRC IRAP publishes no guaranteed funding percentage, practitioner benchmarks report that approved contribution agreements typically reimburse up to 80% of eligible internal technical employee salary costs and up to 50% of eligible arm's-length subcontractor costs. Two institutional facts verify NRC IRAP's 2026 structure: first, Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) transitioned into NRC IRAP's Clean Technology stream in June 2024—which Budget 2025 expanded globally ($39.9 million over four years, $11.1 million ongoing) and Budget 2026 proposed to renew with $298 million over three years starting in 2027–28 ($65 million, $107 million, and $126 million); second, the previously announced plan to fold NRC IRAP into a new Canada Innovation Corporation (CIC) by 2026–2027 stalled with no operational CIC agency or migration underway in 2026, leaving IRAP stably expanding inside the NRC (alongside AI Assist, IP Assist, and defence R&D streams). For larger industrial R&D and biomanufacturing investments, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) administers the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) (such as a $49.9 million biomanufacturing commitment announced in March 2025), complemented for startups by ElevateIP (up to $100,000 in IP services).
Statutory Pool Grinding Mechanics and Correction of Additive Stacking Errors

Under the CRA Qualified Expenditures rules and subsections 127(9), 127(19), and 127(20) of the ITA (plus Bill C-15 technical amendments on government assistance and concessional loans), all government assistance (including NRC IRAP, SIF, and all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits), non-government assistance, and SR&ED contract payments reduce ("grind") qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar in Part 4 of Form T661 before multiplying by the federal 35% or 15% ITC rate. Consequently, promotional guides asserting that a 35% federal ITC plus an 8% Ontario OITC equals a "43% recovery" are mathematically incorrect.

Verified CPA reconciliations demonstrate the exact statutory grinding cascade on $1,000,000 of eligible Ontario current SR&ED expenditures for a qualifying CCPC. In a loss-making year where only the refundable 8% OITC ($80,000) is claimed and no ORDTC is utilized, the $80,000 OITC grinds the federal qualified base to $920,000 ($1,000,000 − $80,000), yielding a 35% federal refundable ITC of $322,000 and a combined cash refund of $402,000—an effective rate of 40.20%, not 43.00%. In a taxable year where the CCPC also utilizes the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC against Ontario tax payable, the $80,000 OITC first grinds the ORDTC base to $920,000, yielding $32,200 of ORDTC (3.5% × $920,000); both Ontario credits then grind the federal base to $887,800 ($1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200), generating $310,730 in federal 35% ITC and a total combined benefit of $422,930 (42.293%, not 46.50%). Conversely, when stacking an illustrative 80% NRC IRAP wage reimbursement ($800,000) onto $1,000,000 of non-specified T4 technical salaries under the Proxy Method (isolating federal SR&ED), the 55% PPA ($550,000) is computed on the unreduced $1,000,000 salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 for a gross pool of $1,550,000, before the $800,000 IRAP grant grinds net federal qualified expenditures in Part 4 to $750,000 ($1,550,000 − $800,000)—generating $262,500 in 35% federal SR&ED cash on top of the $800,000 IRAP contribution for $1,062,500 in combined non-dilutive recovery.

body.text: 7. Governing Agencies, Prescribed Tax Forms, Pre-Claim Approval, and Statutory Deadlines
Institutional Governance, the Absolute 18-Month Deadline, and Preparer Penalties

Tax policy and statutory drafting for federal SR&ED reside with the Department of Finance Canada, while operational administration, scientific/technical eligibility reviews, financial audits, and harmonized provincial credit processing reside with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (alongside Revenu Québec and the Ministère des Finances du Québec in Québec, and Alberta TRA in Alberta). Under the CRA SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy and Guide T4088, claimants must file Form T661 together with Schedule T2SCH31 (corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (individuals) containing all prescribed information within an absolute reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, June 30, 2027 for a December 31, 2025 corporate year-end). There are zero extensions or administrative waivers: missing the 18-month deadline by even a single day permanently forfeits the entire federal SR&ED claim and all T661-dependent provincial credits for that year.

Furthermore, Part 9 of Form T661 mandates full claim-preparer disclosure (covering external consultants—who commonly charge contingency fees of 10% to 25% of approved credits—or lines 935, 970, and 975 certifying purely internal preparation). Per the CRA T2 Corporation Income Tax Guide, if prescribed claim-preparer information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, the claimant and the SR&ED claim preparer are liable, together or separately, for a $1,000 penalty.
CRA Optional Pre-Claim Approval Workflow (Operational April 1, 2026)

Launched on April 1, 2026, the CRA's optional Pre-Claim Approval stream allows eligible businesses to obtain upfront technical validation of planned or recently started SR&ED work before incurring major costs—for up to 3 projects, with each approval valid for up to 3 years (though claimants must still file Form T661 and Schedule 31 after year-end). To qualify, the applicant must be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership with gross business income under $25,000,000 in good standing with the CRA, and the project must neither have been included in a previous SR&ED claim nor involve issues currently under litigation. Applicants follow a three-step workflow:

items: Request a Case Number: Confirm threshold business and project eligibility with the CRA to receive an application case number.
Complete the Technical Application: Answer project eligibility questions and compile supporting project plans and technical documentation.

Upload via My Business Account: Submit the completed application electronically through the CRA My Business Account / SR&ED Client Portal. Published practitioner benchmarks report that the CRA targets an approximately eight-week upfront determination and reduces post-filing expenditure processing to roughly 90 days (compared with 60 to 120 days for standard unreviewed claims and 6 to 18 months for claims selected for full review).

body.text: 8. Judicial Precedents, CRA Eligibility Guidelines, and Audit Defence Standards
Controlling Appellate Jurisprudence on SR&ED Eligibility

Canadian appellate courts enforce a consistent common-law interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the ITA anchored in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (T.C.C.), where Justice Bowman (as he then was) set out five cumulative criteria for SR&ED qualification: (1) whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; (2) whether the claimant formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) whether the procedures adopted accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; (4) whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and (5) whether a detailed contemporaneous record of hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.

The Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) formally endorsed Northwest Hydraulic in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (F.C.A.) (at paragraph 10) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17, following Tax Court findings that a purported hypothesis must be capable of being proved or disproved by scientific research), as well as in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. (2011 FCA) and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. (2016 FCA). At the trial level, Joel Theatrical Rigging (Docket 2015-125(IT)I, January 17, 2017, T.C.C.) dismissed 2008 and 2009 rigging claims (Fire Curtain and Manual Override projects) where activities constituted routine design, pump selection, and valve adjustments, none of the technical PhDs or engineers testified at trial, and physical drop tests failed even to record exact test weights (~800 pounds) or measure acceleration.

More recently, two landmark Federal Court of Appeal decisions closed the door on attempts to relax Northwest Hydraulic. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (May 10, 2021, Webb J.A.), the taxpayer argued that because the words "scientific method" do not appear in subsection 248(1) ITA, the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion should not apply; the FCA unanimously dismissed the appeal, holding that the scientific method is the settled judicial interpretation of "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis". One year later, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (May 2022, Rennie J.A.), the FCA affirmed the denial of a consulting firm's SR&ED claim, reiterating Kam-Press and ruling that an expert witness report cannot rescue a claimant that failed to work methodically and kept only "vague," "unclear" records lacking a logical progression between experimental premise and result.
CRA Eligibility Guidelines and Audit Defence Checklist

Consistent with Kam-Press and National R&D, on August 16, 2021 the CRA replaced its archived eligibility policy with its current Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, framing Northwest Hydraulic into a two-part inquiry: Why the work is conducted (to achieve a scientific or technological advancement resolving technological uncertainty) and How it is conducted (via four elements: generating a hypothesis consistent with known facts, testing that hypothesis through experiment or analysis, developing logical conclusions based on results, and keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses). Claimants should maintain five core audit defence controls throughout each taxation year:

items: Contemporaneous Experimental Documentation: Record technological uncertainties, testable hypotheses, quantitative experimental measurements, iteration logs, and logical conclusions in real time as work progresses rather than reconstructing narratives after year-end.

Granular Payroll and Specified Employee Tracking: Track T4 employee time contemporaneously by SR&ED project, segregate specified employees on lines 305/309, exclude dividends and unpaid wages past 180 days, and file Form T1174 across associated employers.

Environment and Capital Asset Segregation: Separate experimental R&D cloud accounts from production workloads, and maintain ≥90% SR&ED usage logs for post-December 15, 2024 depreciable capital equipment.

Subcontractor Direction and Payment Controls: Contract exclusively with Canadian taxable suppliers for ITC-eligible work, document claimant technical supervision and separate SR&ED line items in contracts, apply the 80% rule strictly to qualifying technical tasks, and pay all non-wage invoices within 180 days of fiscal year-end.

Direct Technical Witness Readiness and Objection Preservation: Ensure qualified in-house engineers or scientists prepare Part 2 of Form T661 and participate directly in CRA technical reviews (avoiding the Joel Theatrical Rigging evidentiary failure), and serve any formal Notice of Objection within the statutory Part I objection period.
